modern:
The psalmist felt his need of God’s guidance. He had just been discovering the foolishness of his own heart, and so that he wouldn’t keep being led astray by it, he resolved that from now on God’s counsel would guide him. A sense of our own folly is a great step toward being wise, when it leads us to rely on the wisdom of the Lord. The blind man leans on his friend’s arm and gets home safely, and that is how we would give ourselves up completely to God’s guidance, not doubting at all, sure that though we can’t see, it is always safe to trust the all-seeing God. “*Thou shalt*” is a blessed expression of confidence. He was sure that the Lord wouldn’t turn down the gracious task of stooping to guide him.

There is a word for you, believer; rest in it. Be sure that your God will be your counselor and friend; he will guide you; he will direct all your ways. In his written Word you already have this promise partly kept, for holy Scripture is his counsel to you. How happy we are to have God’s Word always there to guide us! What would the sailor be without his compass? And what would the Christian be without the Bible? This is the chart that never errs, the map on which every sandbank is drawn, and all the channels from the quicksands of destruction to the harbor of salvation are mapped and marked by one who knows the whole way. Blessed be you, O God, that we may trust you to guide us now, and guide us right to the end!

After this guidance through life, the psalmist looks forward to God’s welcome at last: “*and afterward receive me to glory*.” What a thought for you, believer! God himself will receive *you* to glory—*you*! Wandering, erring, straying, yet he will bring you safely to glory at last! This is your portion; live on it today, and if perplexities surround you, go in the strength of this text straight to the throne.

notes.term: Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory
notes.note: [[Ps.73.24|Psalm 73:24]]. The psalm is Asaph’s. He had nearly lost his footing envying the wicked, until he went into God’s sanctuary and confessed, “So foolish was I, and ignorant” ([[Ps.73.22|Psalm 73:22]]).
Completely, without question.
Stooping down from a high position, in the good sense, without today’s sense of looking down on someone.
A sailor.
A sandbank or shallow place where a ship can run aground.
A harbor.
A share of an inheritance. When God is “our portion”, he himself is what we inherit, and he is enough.
The throne of grace, where believers come to God in prayer: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” ([[Heb.4.16|Hebrews 4:16]]).

modern: Faith is as much the rule of everyday life as of spiritual life. We ought to have faith in God for our earthly affairs as well as for our heavenly business. Only as we learn to trust God to supply all our daily needs will we live above the world. We aren’t to be idle; *that* would show we did *not* trust in God, who is always at work, but in the devil, who is the father of idleness. We aren’t to be careless or rash; that would be trusting chance, and not the living God, who is a God of careful management and order. Acting with all good sense and honesty, we are to rely simply and entirely on the Lord at all times.

Let me recommend to you a life of trusting God in practical things. If you trust God, you won’t have to grieve over using sinful means to get rich. Serve God with integrity, and if you achieve no success, at least there will be no sin on your conscience. If you trust God, you won’t be guilty of contradicting yourself. The person who trusts in cunning sails this way today and that way tomorrow, like a ship tossed about by the changeable wind; but the one who trusts in the Lord is like a steamship: she cuts through the waves, defies the wind, and leaves one bright, silvery, straight track to the harbor she is bound for. Be someone with living principles inside you; never bow to the shifting customs of worldly wisdom. Walk your path of integrity with steady steps, and show that you are unbeatably strong in the strength that only confidence in God can give.

That way you will be set free from anxious care. You won’t be troubled by bad news; your heart will be fixed, trusting in the Lord. How pleasant to float along the stream of providence! There is no more blessed way of living than a life of depending on a covenant-keeping God. We have no cares, for he cares for us; we have no troubles, because we cast our burdens on the Lord.

notes.term: Trust in him at all times
notes.note: “Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us” ([[Ps.62.8|Psalm 62:8]]).
Belonging to this life, as opposed to eternity.
Who has always been at work. “My Father worketh hitherto, and I work” ([[John.5.17|John 5:17]]).

notes.term: A God of economy and order
notes.note: Economy here means careful management, not only saving money.
Cunning, trickery.
A steamship, still something of a wonder in Spurgeon’s day: it could hold its course whatever the wind, where a sailing ship couldn’t.

notes.term: Your heart will be fixed, trusting in the Lord
notes.note: “He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD” ([[Ps.112.7|Psalm 112:7]]).
God’s care and control over everything that happens, providing for his people.
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” ([[1Pet.5.7|1 Peter 5:7]]).

modern:
This little peek into the house of the fisherman apostle is very interesting. We see at once that household joys and cares are no obstacle to the full work of ministry. More than that, since they give a minister the chance to see the Lord’s gracious work on his own flesh and blood, they may teach the teacher better than any other earthly training. Roman Catholics and other sects may run down marriage, but true Christianity and family life go well together. Peter’s house was probably a poor fisherman’s hut, but the Lord of Glory went into it, stayed in it and worked a miracle in it. If our little book is being read this morning in some very humble cottage, let this fact encourage the people who live there to seek the company of King Jesus. God is more often in little huts than in rich palaces. Jesus is looking around your room now, and is waiting to be gracious to you.

Sickness had come into Simon’s house. Fever in a deadly form had laid his mother-in-law low, and as soon as Jesus came they told him about the sad trouble, and he hurried to the patient’s bed. Is there any sickness in your house this morning? You will find Jesus by far the best physician; go to him at once and tell him all about it. Lay the case before him immediately. It concerns one of his people, so it won’t be trivial to him. Notice that the Savior restored the sick woman at once; no one can heal the way he does. We can’t be sure that the Lord will at once remove all disease from those we love, but we can know that believing prayer for the sick is far more likely to be followed by recovery than anything else in the world; and where it doesn’t succeed, we must humbly bow to the will of the one who decides life and death. The tender heart of Jesus is waiting to hear our griefs; let’s pour them into his patient ear.

notes.note: At once, straight away.
Spurgeon’s word, common among Protestants of his day, for Roman Catholics. He has in mind the rule that priests must not marry, while Peter, the apostle they claim as their first pope, had a wife.
Members of sects.
Run down, speak against.
Worked.
In older English, simply the people living in a house, not prisoners.
“And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you” ([[Isa.30.18|Isaiah 30:18]]).
Laid low; knocked flat.
Where it doesn’t succeed.

modern:
A craving for marvels was a sign of how sickly people’s minds were in our Lord’s day. They refused solid food and pined for mere wonders. The gospel, which they needed so badly, they wouldn’t have; the miracles, which Jesus didn’t always choose to give, they eagerly demanded. Many today must see signs and wonders or they won’t believe. Some have said in their hearts, “I must feel deep horror of soul, or I never will believe in Jesus.” But what if you never feel it, as you probably never will? Will you go to hell out of spite against God, because he won’t treat you like someone else? Another has said to himself, “If I had a dream, or if I could feel a sudden shock of I know not what, then I would believe.” So you undeserving mortals imagine that my Lord is to take orders from you! You are beggars at his gate, asking for mercy, and you must draw up rules and regulations for how he is to give that mercy. Do you think he will put up with this? My Master has a generous spirit, but he has a truly royal heart; he spurns all dictation and keeps his sovereign freedom to act.

Why, dear reader, if this is your case, do you crave signs and wonders? Isn’t the gospel its own sign and wonder? Isn’t this a miracle of miracles, that “God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him might not perish”? Surely that precious word, “Whosoever will, let him come and take the water of life freely,” and that solemn promise, “Him that cometh unto me, I will in no wise cast out,” are better than signs and wonders! A truthful Savior ought to be believed. He is truth itself. Why would you ask for proof that the one who can’t lie is telling the truth? The demons themselves declared him to be the Son of God; will you distrust him?

notes.term: Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe
notes.note: Jesus to a royal official who begged him to come and heal his dying son. The man believed Jesus’ word, went home, and found his son well ([[John.4.46-John.4.53|John 4:46–53]]).
God’s right and power to rule and to choose freely, answering to no one.
[[John.3.16|John 3:16]], quoted from memory. The verse says “should not perish, but have everlasting life.”

notes.term: Whosoever will, let him come and take the water of life freely
notes.note: [[Rev.22.17|Revelation 22:17]], quoted from memory. The verse reads “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.”
Truthfulness.
“In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began” ([[Titus.1.2|Titus 1:2]]).

notes.term: The devils themselves declared him to be the Son of God
notes.note: “And devils also came out of many, crying out, and saying, Thou art Christ the Son of God” ([[Luke.4.41|Luke 4:41]]).

modern: It is good to be able to say of the Lord Jesus, without any “if” or “but”: “*Thou whom my soul loveth*.” Many can only say of Jesus that they *hope* they love him, or they *trust* they love him; but only a poor and shallow experience will be content to stop there. No one should give his spirit any rest until he is quite sure about something so vitally important. We shouldn’t be satisfied with a shallow *hope* that Jesus loves us, and a bare trust that we love him. The old saints didn’t usually talk in “buts,” and “ifs,” and “hopes,” and “trusts”; they spoke positively and plainly. “I know whom I have believed,” says Paul. “I know that my Redeemer liveth,” says Job. Get positive knowledge of your love for Jesus, and don’t be satisfied until you can speak of your share in him as a reality. You make sure of it by receiving the witness of the Holy Spirit, and his seal on your soul by faith.

True love for Christ is always the Holy Spirit’s work, and he must produce it in the heart. He is the *efficient cause* of it; but the logical reason we love Jesus lies in *himself*. *Why* do we love Jesus? *Because he first loved us*. *Why* do we love Jesus? Because he “*gave himself for us*.” We have life through his death; we have peace through his blood. Though he was rich, *for our sakes* he became poor. Why do we love Jesus? Because of the *excellence of his person*. We are filled with a sense of his beauty, an admiration of his charms, an awareness of his infinite perfection! His greatness, goodness and loveliness combine in one dazzling ray to enchant the soul, until it is so carried away that it exclaims, “Yea, he is altogether lovely.” Blessed love this: a love that binds the heart with chains softer than silk, and yet firmer than diamond!

notes.note: The bride speaking of the one she loves: “Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest” ([[Song.1.7|Song of Solomon 1:7]]). Christians have long read the Song as a picture of Christ and his people.

notes.term: I know whom I have believed
I know that my Redeemer liveth

notes.note: A share in him; a stake in all that is his.
The Holy Spirit marks believers as God’s own, the way a seal marks property: “ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” ([[Eph.1.13|Ephesians 1:13]]).
An old term from philosophy: the one who actually brings something about.
“We love him, because he first loved us” ([[1John.4.19|1 John 4:19]]).
“Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity” ([[Titus.2.14|Titus 2:14]]).

notes.term: For our sakes he became poor
notes.note: [[2Cor.8.9|2 Corinthians 8:9]].
Carried away with delight.
[[Song.5.16|Song of Solomon 5:16]].
An old name for the hardest stone, often meaning diamond.

modern:
All events are under the control of providence, so all the trials of our outward life can be traced straight back to the great First Cause. Out of the golden gate of God’s decree the armies of trial march out in battle order, dressed in iron armor and carrying weapons of war. Every providence is a door to trial. Even our mercies, like roses, have their thorns. People can drown in seas of prosperity as well as in rivers of affliction. No mountain of ours is too high, and no valley too low, for temptations: trials lurk on every road. Everywhere, above and below, we are hemmed in and surrounded by dangers. Yet no shower falls from the threatening cloud without permission; every drop has its orders before it hurries to the earth.

The trials that come from God are sent to prove and strengthen our graces. In this way they show the power of God’s grace, test whether our virtues are genuine, and add to their energy. Our Lord, in his infinite wisdom and overflowing love, sets so high a value on his people’s faith that he won’t shield them from the trials that strengthen it. You would never have had the precious faith that now holds you up if the trial of your faith hadn’t been like fire. You are a tree that would never have rooted so well if the wind hadn’t rocked you back and forth, and made you take firm hold of the precious truths of covenant grace. Worldly ease is a great enemy of faith; it loosens the joints of holy courage and snaps the sinews of sacred bravery. The balloon never rises until the ropes are cut; affliction does this sharp service for believing souls. While the wheat sleeps comfortably in the husk it is useless to us; it must be threshed out of its resting place before its value can be known. So it is good that Jehovah tests the righteous, for it makes them grow rich toward God.

notes.note: “The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth” ([[Ps.11.5|Psalm 11:5]]). Trieth means tests.
God’s care and control over everything that happens, providing for his people.
God, the cause behind every other cause.
What God has decreed (not here the ordinances of the church).
The good qualities the Spirit grows in a believer, such as faith, love and patience.
“That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire” ([[1Pet.1.7|1 Peter 1:7]]).
God’s binding promise to save his people through Christ, freely, as a gift and not a reward.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
“So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God” ([[Luke.12.21|Luke 12:21]]).

modern:
The darkness at the beginning of time heard the Almighty’s command, “light be,” and at once there was light; and the word of the Lord Jesus is equal in majesty to that ancient word of power. Redemption, like creation, has its mighty word. Jesus speaks, and it is done. Leprosy gave way to no human remedy, but it fled at once at the Lord’s “I will.” The disease showed no hopeful signs of recovery, and nature contributed nothing to its own healing, but the word alone did the entire work, on the spot and for ever. The sinner is in a worse plight than the leper; let him follow the leper’s example and go to Jesus, “beseeching him and kneeling down to him.” Let him use whatever little faith he has, even if it goes no further than “Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean”; and there need be no doubt about how his request will turn out. Jesus heals all who come, and turns none away.

In reading the story our text this morning comes from, it is worth noticing reverently that Jesus touched the leper. This unclean man had broken through the rules of the ceremonial law and pushed his way into the house, but Jesus, far from scolding him, broke through the law himself to meet him. He made an exchange with the leper: while he cleansed him, by that touch he took on himself a ceremonial uncleanness. In the same way Jesus Christ was made sin for us, although in himself he knew no sin, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Oh, that poor sinners would go to Jesus, believing in the power of his blessed work as their substitute! They would soon learn the power of his gracious touch. That hand which multiplied the loaves, which saved sinking Peter, which holds up suffering saints, which crowns believers—that same hand will touch every seeking sinner, and in a moment make him clean. The love of Jesus is the source of salvation. He loves, he looks, he touches us, *we live*.

notes.note: Jesus to a leper who knelt and said, “If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean” ([[Mark.1.40-Mark.1.42|Mark 1:40–42]]).
From the very beginning of time.
A command. It is Latin for “let it be”: the Latin Bible’s “Let there be light” is *fiat lux* ([[Gen.1.3|Genesis 1:3]]).

notes.term: Beseeching him and kneeling down to him
notes.note: [[Mark.1.40|Mark 1:40]]. Beseeching means begging.
The laws of Moses about clean and unclean, sacrifices and festivals. A leper had to live apart and cry “Unclean, unclean” ([[Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46|Leviticus 13:45–46]]).
Uncleanness under the laws of Leviticus. Touching a leper made a person ceremonially unclean.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” ([[2Cor.5.21|2 Corinthians 5:21]]).
One taking another’s place: here, Christ taking the punishment due to sinners.

modern: Weights, scales and measures were all to meet the standard of justice. Surely no Christian will need reminding of this in his business, for if honesty were driven out of all the rest of the world, it should find shelter in believing hearts. There are, however, other scales that weigh moral and spiritual things, and these often need inspecting. We’ll call in the inspector tonight.

The scales we weigh our own character and other people’s in: are they quite accurate? Don’t we turn our own ounces of goodness into pounds, and other people’s bushels of excellence into pecks? Check the weights and measures here, Christian. The scales we weigh our trials and troubles in: are they up to standard? Paul, who had more to suffer than we have, called his afflictions light, and yet we often think ours are heavy—surely something must be wrong with the weights! We must look into this, or we may be reported to the court above for dishonest dealing.

The weights we measure our beliefs about doctrine with: are they quite fair? The doctrines of grace should carry the same weight with us as the commands of the Word, no more and no less; but it is to be feared that with many people one scale or the other is unfairly weighted. It is a grand thing to give just measure in truth. Christian, be careful here.

The measures we use to estimate our duties and responsibilities look rather small. When a rich man gives no more to God’s cause than the poor do, is that a just ephah and a just hin? When ministers are half starved, is that honest dealing? When the poor are despised while ungodly rich men are admired, is that a just balance? Reader, we could make the list longer, but we prefer to leave it as your evening’s work to find and destroy all dishonest balances, weights and measures.

notes.note: A dry measure for grain, about two-thirds of a bushel.
A measure for liquids, about a gallon.
Scales with two pans, for weighing.
The inspector of weights and measures, who checked that shopkeepers’ scales were honest.
A peck is a quarter of a bushel.
“For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” ([[2Cor.4.17|2 Corinthians 4:17]]).
The teachings that salvation is God’s free gift from start to finish: his choosing, Christ’s redeeming, and the Spirit’s calling and keeping.
Commands.

modern:
As a Christian you have to live in the middle of an ungodly world, and it does you little good to cry, “Woe is me.” Jesus didn’t pray that you would be taken out of the world, and what he didn’t pray for, you don’t need to want. Far better, in the Lord’s strength, to meet the difficulty and glorify him in it. The enemy is always watching to catch you being inconsistent, so be very *holy*. Remember that all eyes are on you, and that more is expected of you than of other people. Try hard to give no cause for blame. Let your goodness be the only fault they can find in you. Like Daniel, make them say of you, “We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”

Try to be *useful* as well as consistent. Perhaps you think, “If I were in a better position I might serve the Lord’s cause, but I can’t do any good where I am.” But the worse the people you live among, the more they need your efforts. If they are crooked, all the more reason you should set them straight; and if they are stubborn, all the more need for you to turn their proud hearts to the truth. Where should the doctor be but where there are many sick? Where is a soldier to win honor but in the hottest fire of the battle?

And when you are weary of the strife and sin that meet you on every side, remember that all the saints have gone through the same trial. They weren’t carried to heaven on feather beds, and you mustn’t expect to travel more easily than they did. They had to risk their lives to the death on the front line of the battlefield, and you won’t be crowned until you too have endured hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. So “stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.”

notes.term: Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech
notes.note: The psalmist laments living among hostile people far from home ([[Ps.120.5-Ps.120.7|Psalm 120:5–7]]). Mesech and Kedar were distant peoples, here standing for unfriendly neighbors. To sojourn is to live somewhere as a stranger.

notes.term: Jesus did not pray that you should be taken out of the world
notes.note: “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” ([[John.17.15|John 17:15]]).

notes.term: We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel
notes.note: Daniel’s enemies at the Persian court, who could find no fault in him except his faith ([[Dan.6.5|Daniel 6:5]]). Occasion means grounds for complaint.
Stubbornly wrong; contrary.
Soft feather beds. An echo of Isaac Watts’ hymn: “Must I be carried to the skies / On flowery beds of ease?”

notes.term: The high places of the field
notes.note: The front line of the battle. Zebulun and Naphtali “jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field” ([[Judg.5.18|Judges 5:18]]).

notes.term: Endured hardness as a good soldier of Jesus Christ
notes.note: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ” ([[2Tim.2.3|2 Timothy 2:3]]). Hardness means hardship.

notes.term: Stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong
notes.note: [[1Cor.16.13|1 Corinthians 16:13]]. To “quit you like men” is to act like men: be brave.

modern:
Some things in nature must remain a mystery to the most intelligent and adventurous researchers. Human knowledge has limits it can’t pass. Knowledge of everything belongs to God alone. If this is so in the things that are seen and temporary, I can be sure it is even more so in spiritual and eternal matters. Why, then, have I been racking my brain with theories about destiny and will, fixed fate and human responsibility? These deep and dark truths are no more within my grasp than the depths that lie hidden below, from which old ocean draws her watery stores. Why am I so curious to know the reason for my Lord’s providences, the motive of his actions, the purpose of his visits? Will I ever be able to clasp the sun in my fist, and hold the universe in my palm? Yet these are like a drop in a bucket compared with the Lord my God.

Let me not strain to understand the infinite, but spend my strength in love. What I can’t gain by intellect I can possess by affection, and let that be enough for me. I can’t get into the heart of the sea, but I can enjoy the healthy breezes that sweep across its surface, and I can sail its blue waves with favorable winds. If I could enter the springs of the sea, the feat would do no good to me or anyone else. It wouldn’t save the sinking ship, or give the drowned sailor back to his weeping wife and children. Nor would solving deep mysteries do me the slightest good, for the least love for God, and the simplest act of obedience to him, are better than the deepest knowledge. My Lord, I leave the infinite to you, and I pray that you would keep me far from such a love for the tree of knowledge as might keep me from the tree of life.

notes.term: Hast thou entered into the springs of the sea?
notes.note: God questioning Job out of the whirlwind: “or hast thou walked in the search of the depth?” ([[Job.38.16|Job 38:16]]).

notes.term: The things which are seen and temporal
notes.note: “For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” ([[2Cor.4.18|2 Corinthians 4:18]]). Temporal means lasting only for a time.

Old puzzles about God’s plan and human choice. An echo of Milton’s fallen angels, who argued of “Fixed fate, free will, foreknowledge absolute, / And found no end, in wandering mazes lost” (*Paradise Lost*, Book 2).
Lies hidden.
Times when God comes to deal with someone, often in trial.
“Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket” ([[Isa.40.15|Isaiah 40:15]]).
In older English, the heart’s loves and desires, not only fondness.
The chest, the place of closest embrace. Here, the surface of the sea.
Favorable.
A ship.

notes.term: The tree of knowledge… the tree of life
notes.note: The two trees in Eden ([[Gen.2.9|Genesis 2:9]]). Reaching for the first cost Adam the second ([[Gen.3.22-Gen.3.24|Genesis 3:22–24]]).

modern:
We use lights to *make things visible*. A Christian should shine in his life so that no one could live with him for a week without learning the gospel. His conduct should be such that everyone around him clearly sees whose he is and whom he serves, and sees the image of Jesus reflected in his daily actions.

Lights are meant for *guidance*. We are to help those around us who are in the dark. We are to hold out the Word of life to them. We are to point sinners to the Savior, and the weary to God’s own resting place. People sometimes read their Bibles and don’t understand them; we should be ready, like Philip, to teach the inquirer the meaning of God’s Word, the way of salvation and the life of godliness.

Lights are also used for *warning*. A lighthouse is sure to be built on our rocks and sandbanks. Christians should know that false lights are shown everywhere in the world, so the right light is needed. Satan’s wreckers are always out, tempting the ungodly to sin under the name of pleasure. They hoist the wrong light; let it be ours to put up the true light on every dangerous rock, to point out every sin and tell what it leads to, so that we may be clear of the blood of all men, shining as lights in the world.

Lights also have a very *cheering* influence, and so do Christians. A Christian ought to be a comforter, with kind words on his lips and sympathy in his heart. He should carry sunshine wherever he goes, and spread happiness around him.

notes.term: Among whom ye shine as lights in the world
notes.note: “That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation” ([[Phil.2.15|Philippians 2:15]]).
Make visible; show.
In older English, your whole way of life, not only your talk.

notes.term: Hold forth to them the Word of life
notes.note: “Holding forth the word of life” ([[Phil.2.16|Philippians 2:16]]).
Philip explained Isaiah to an Ethiopian official who was reading it in his chariot, asking him, “Understandest thou what thou readest?” ([[Acts.8.30-Acts.8.35|Acts 8:30–35]]).
Wreckers were people on dangerous coasts who were said to show false lights to lure ships onto the rocks, so they could plunder the wrecks.

notes.term: Clear of the blood of all men
notes.note: Paul to the Ephesian elders: “I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” ([[Acts.20.26-Acts.20.27|Acts 20:26–27]]).
Spread.

modern:
Whoever looks at his own character and standing from the law’s point of view will not only despair when he gets to the *end* of his reckoning; if he is wise, he will despair at the *beginning*. For if we are to be judged on the basis of the law, no one alive will be justified. How blessed to know that we live in the realm of grace and not of law! When I think about my state before God, the question isn’t, “Am I perfect in myself before the law?” but, “Am I perfect in Christ Jesus?” That is a very different matter. We don’t need to ask, “Am I without sin naturally?” but, “Have I been washed in the fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness?” It isn’t “Am I in myself well pleasing to God?” but “Am I accepted in the Beloved?”

The Christian looks at his evidences from the top of Sinai and grows alarmed about his salvation; he would do far better to read his title deed by the light of Calvary. “Why,” he says, “my faith has unbelief in it, it is not able to save me.” If he had looked at *the object* of his faith instead of his faith, he would have said, “There is no failure in *him*, and therefore I am safe.” He sighs over his hope: “Ah! my hope is marred and dimmed by an anxious carefulness about present things; how can I be accepted?” If he had looked at *the ground* of his hope, he would have seen that God’s promise stands firm, and that whatever our doubts may be, the oath and the promise never fail.

Ah, believer, it is always safer for you to be led by the Spirit into gospel freedom than to wear the chains of the law. Judge yourself by what *Christ* is rather than by what *you* are. Satan will try to spoil your peace by reminding you of your sinfulness and imperfections; you can only meet his accusations by holding faithfully to the gospel and refusing to wear the yoke of slavery.

notes.term: If ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law
notes.note: [[Gal.5.18|Galatians 5:18]].

notes.note: “For in thy sight shall no man living be justified” ([[Ps.143.2|Psalm 143:2]]); “by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified” ([[Gal.2.16|Galatians 2:16]]).

notes.note: [[Zech.13.1|Zechariah 13:1]].

notes.note: Sinai, where the law was given, stands for judging yourself by the law; Calvary, where Christ died, for trusting his finished work.

God backed his promise with an oath, “that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation” ([[Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18|Hebrews 6:17–18]]).

“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” ([[Gal.5.1|Galatians 5:1]]).

modern: *Faith is full of inventions*. The house was full, and a crowd blocked the door, but faith found a way to get at the Lord and put the paralyzed man in front of him. If we can’t get sinners to where Jesus is by ordinary methods, we must use extraordinary ones. It seems, according to [[Luke.5.19|Luke 5:19]], that tiles had to be taken off, which would make dust and put the people below in some danger; but when the case is very urgent we mustn’t mind running some risks and shocking some sense of propriety. Jesus was there to heal, and so, come what may, faith risked everything so that her poor paralyzed charge might have his sins forgiven. Oh, that we had more daring faith among us! Dear reader, can’t we seek it this morning for ourselves and for our fellow workers? And won’t we try today to do some gallant act for the love of souls and the glory of the Lord?

The world is always inventing; genius serves every purpose of human desire. Can’t faith invent too, and reach by some new means the outcasts who lie perishing around us? It was the presence of Jesus that stirred up winning courage in the four men who carried the paralyzed man. Isn’t the Lord among us now? Have we seen his face for ourselves this morning? Have we felt his healing power in our own souls? If so, then through door, through window or through roof, let’s break through every obstacle and work to bring poor souls to Jesus. All means are good and fitting when faith and love are truly set on winning souls. If hunger for bread can break through stone walls, surely hunger for souls won’t be held back in its efforts. O Lord, make us quick to think of ways of reaching your poor sin-sick ones, and bold to carry them out at any risk.

notes.term: They uncovered the roof where he was
notes.note: Four men carried a paralyzed friend to Jesus, and when the crowd blocked the way they opened the roof and let him down. Jesus forgave his sins and healed him ([[Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12|Mark 2:1–12]]).
Near.
The crowd.
Paralyzed. Palsy is an old word for paralysis.
The rules of polite behavior.
Whatever happened; come what may.
Proper, fitting.

notes.term: Hunger for bread can break through stone walls
notes.note: From the old proverb “Hunger breaks stone walls.”

modern:
We know little of what sorrow may be on the sea at this moment. We are safe in our quiet room, but far away on the salt sea the hurricane may be cruelly hunting for people’s lives. Listen to the demons of death howling in the rigging, and every timber springing as the waves pound the ship like battering rams! God help you, poor drenched and worn-out ones! My prayer goes up to the great Lord of sea and land, that he will make the storm a calm and bring you to your desired harbor! And I shouldn’t only pray; I should try to help those hardy men who risk their lives so constantly. Have I ever done anything for them? What can I do?

How often the raging sea swallows up the sailor! Thousands of bodies lie where pearls lie deep. There is the sorrow of death on the sea, echoed in the long wail of widows and orphans. The salt of the sea is in the eyes of many mothers and wives. Pitiless waves, you have devoured the men women loved, and the mainstay of households. What a resurrection there will be from the caverns of the deep when the sea gives up her dead! Until then there will be sorrow on the sea.

As if in sympathy with the troubles of the earth, the sea is forever fretting along a thousand shores, wailing with a sorrowful cry like her own birds, booming with a hollow crash of unrest, raving with uproarious discontent, chafing with hoarse anger, or jangling with the voices of ten thousand murmuring pebbles. The roar of the sea may be joyful to a rejoicing spirit, but to the son of sorrow the wide, wide ocean is even more lonely than the wide, wide world. This isn’t our rest, and the restless waves tell us so. There is a land where there is no more sea, and our faces are firmly set toward it; we are going to the place the Lord has spoken of. Until then, we cast our sorrows on the Lord who walked on the sea long ago, and who makes a way for his people through its depths.

notes.term: There is sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet
notes.note: From Jeremiah’s prophecy against Damascus ([[Jer.49.23|Jeremiah 49:23]]).
A ship’s ropes and rigging.
“He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still… so he bringeth them unto their desired haven” ([[Ps.107.29-Ps.107.30|Psalm 107:29–30]]).

notes.note: “And the sea gave up the dead which were in it” ([[Rev.20.13|Revelation 20:13]]).
“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth… and there was no more sea” ([[Rev.21.1|Revelation 21:1]]).

notes.term: The place of which the Lord hath spoken
notes.note: Moses to his father-in-law: “We are journeying unto the place of which the LORD said, I will give it you” ([[Num.10.29|Numbers 10:29]]).

notes.note: Jesus walked on the Sea of Galilee ([[Matt.14.25|Matthew 14:25]]).

notes.note: “Art thou not it which hath dried the sea… that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over?” ([[Isa.51.10|Isaiah 51:10]]).

modern: Our fruit comes from our God by way of *union*. The fruit of the branch can be traced directly back to the root. Cut the connection and the branch dies, and no fruit is produced. Because of our union with Christ we bear fruit. Every bunch of grapes was first in the root; it passed through the stem and flowed through the sap vessels, and shaped itself outwardly into fruit, but it was in the stem first. In the same way every good work was first in Christ, and then is brought out in us. Christian, treasure this precious union with Christ; it must be the source of all the fruitfulness you can hope to know. If you weren’t joined to Jesus Christ, you would be a barren branch indeed.

Our fruit comes from God by way of *spiritual providence*. When the dewdrops fall from heaven, when the cloud looks down from on high about to let fall its liquid treasure, when the bright sun swells the grapes of the cluster, each heavenly gift may whisper to the tree, “From me is thy fruit found.” The fruit owes much to the root, which is essential to fruitfulness, but it also owes a great deal to outside influences. How much we owe to God’s providence of grace! Through it he constantly supplies us with new life, teaching, comfort, strength or whatever else we need. To this we owe all our usefulness and virtue.

Our fruit comes from God by way of *wise gardening*. The gardener’s sharp knife makes the tree more fruitful by thinning the clusters and cutting off unneeded shoots. So it is, Christian, with the pruning the Lord gives you. “My Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away; and every branch that beareth fruit he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.” Since our God is the author of our spiritual graces, let’s give him all the glory of our salvation.

notes.term: From me is thy fruit found
notes.note: God’s closing word to Israel in Hosea: “I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found” ([[Hos.14.8|Hosea 14:8]]).
Let fall in drops.
A gift; a blessing.
To make alive. “Quick” once meant “living”, as in “the quick and the dead”.
Comfort.
Farming and gardening; the care of crops and vines. A husbandman is a farmer or vinedresser.
[[John.15.1-John.15.2|John 15:1–2]]. Purgeth means prunes and cleans.
The good qualities the Spirit grows in a believer, such as faith, love and patience.

modern:
In the resurrection of Christ, as in our salvation, nothing less than *divine power* was at work. What can we say of those who think conversion is brought about by man’s free will, and is due to his own better nature? When we see the dead rise from the grave by their own power, then we may expect to see ungodly sinners turning to Christ of their own free will. It isn’t the word preached, or the word read, in itself; all life-giving power comes from the Holy Spirit.

This power was *irresistible*. All the soldiers and the high priests couldn’t keep the body of Christ in the tomb; Death himself couldn’t hold Jesus in his chains. Just as irresistible is the power at work in the believer when he is raised to newness of life. No sin, no corruption, no devils in hell or sinners on earth can stop the hand of God’s grace when it means to convert someone. If God in his almighty power says, “Thou shalt,” man won’t say, “I will not.”

Notice that the power that raised Christ from the dead was *glorious*. It brought honor to God and struck dismay into the armies of evil. So there is great glory to God in the conversion of every sinner. It was *everlasting power*. “Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.” So we, having been raised from the dead, don’t go back to our dead works or our old corruptions; we live to God. “Because he lives we live also.” “For we are dead, and our life is hid with Christ in God.” “Like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.” Lastly, notice in the text *the union of the new life to Jesus*. The same power that raised the Head brings life to the members. What a blessing to be made alive together with Christ!

notes.term: The exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe
notes.note: [[Eph.1.19-Eph.1.20|Ephesians 1:19–20]]. To us-ward means toward us.
A better nature or temperament.
To make alive. “Quick” once meant “living”, as in “the quick and the dead”.
The sinful desires still at work in a believer.
With all-powerful authority.

notes.term: Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more
notes.note: [[Rom.6.9|Romans 6:9]].

notes.term: Because he lives we live also
notes.note: Jesus’ words, quoted from memory: “because I live, ye shall live also” ([[John.14.19|John 14:19]]).

notes.term: For we are dead, and our life is hid with Christ in God
notes.note: Quoted from memory. Paul writes, “For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God” ([[Col.3.3|Colossians 3:3]]).

notes.term: Like as Christ was raised up from the dead
notes.note: [[Rom.6.4|Romans 6:4]].
“Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ” ([[Eph.2.5|Ephesians 2:5]]).

modern:
There are different translations of these words. One version renders it, “I will shew thee great and fortified things.” Another, “Great and reserved things.” Now, there are reserved and special things in Christian experience: not every stage of spiritual life is equally easy to reach. There are the ordinary frames and feelings of repentance, faith, joy and hope, which the whole family enjoys; but there is an upper realm of rapture, of communion and of conscious union with Christ, which is far from being where believers usually live. Not all of us have John’s high privilege of leaning on Jesus’ chest, or Paul’s of being caught up into the third heaven. There are heights in the experienced knowledge of the things of God that the eagle eye of sharp intellect and philosophical thought has never seen. God alone can carry us there; but the chariot he takes us up in, and the fiery horses that pull it, are prevailing prayers.

Prevailing prayer overcomes even the God of mercy: “By his strength he had power with God: yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Beth-el, and there he spake with us.” Prevailing prayer takes the Christian to Carmel, and enables him to cover heaven with clouds of blessing and the earth with floods of mercy. Prevailing prayer lifts the Christian up to Pisgah and shows him the inheritance kept for him; it raises us to Tabor and transfigures us, until in the likeness of his Lord, as he is, so are we also in this world. If you want to reach something higher than ordinary, earthbound experience, look to the Rock that is higher than you, and gaze with the eye of faith through the window of persistent prayer. When you open the window on your side, it won’t be bolted on the other.

notes.term: Great and mighty things which thou knowest not
notes.note: “Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things” ([[Jer.33.3|Jeremiah 33:3]]). The Hebrew word for “mighty” can mean fortified or hidden, which is why versions differ.
States of mind and heart.
At the Last Supper, John was “leaning on Jesus’ bosom” ([[John.13.23|John 13:23]]).

notes.term: Caught up into the third heaven
notes.note: [[2Cor.12.2|2 Corinthians 12:2]].
Known by personal experience, not only taught.
Sharpness of mind.
Like the chariot and horses of fire that took Elijah up to heaven ([[2Kgs.2.11|2 Kings 2:11]]).

notes.term: By his strength he had power with God
notes.note: Jacob wrestling with the angel ([[Hos.12.3-Hos.12.4|Hosea 12:3–4]]; [[Gen.32.24-Gen.32.28|Genesis 32:24–28]]). Supplication means humble, earnest prayer.

Three mountains. On Carmel, Elijah prayed until a little cloud became a downpour ([[1Kgs.18.42-1Kgs.18.45|1 Kings 18:42–45]]). From Pisgah, Moses saw the promised land ([[Deut.34.1-Deut.34.4|Deuteronomy 34:1–4]]). Tabor was long thought to be the mountain where Jesus was transfigured ([[Matt.17.1-Matt.17.2|Matthew 17:1–2]]).

notes.term: The Rock that is higher than you
notes.note: “Lead me to the rock that is higher than I” ([[Ps.61.2|Psalm 61:2]]).
Persistent; refusing to give up asking.

modern: These representatives of the saints in heaven are said to be *around the throne*. In the passage in the Song of Solomon where Solomon sings of the King sitting at his table, some translate it “a round table.” From this, some interpreters have said, without straining the text, I think, “There is an equality among the saints.” That idea is conveyed by the equal nearness of the twenty-four elders. The state of glorified spirits in heaven is one of nearness to Christ, clear sight of his glory, constant access to his court and familiar fellowship with his person. And there is no difference in this between one saint and another. All the people of God, apostles, martyrs, ministers, or private and unknown Christians, will all be seated *near the throne*, where they will gaze on their exalted Lord forever and be satisfied with his love. They will all be near to Christ, all carried away by his love, all eating and drinking at the same table with him, all equally loved as his favorites and friends, even if not all equally rewarded as servants.

Let believers on earth imitate the saints in heaven in their nearness to Christ. Let’s be on earth what the elders are in heaven, sitting around the throne. May Christ be the object of our thoughts and the center of our lives. How can we bear to live so far from the one we love? Lord Jesus, draw us nearer to yourself. Say to us, “Abide in me, and I in you”; and let us sing, “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”

notes.note: Twenty-four elders ([[Rev.4.4|Revelation 4:4]]).
Clothing.
Another name for the Song of Solomon.

notes.term: The King sitting at his table
notes.note: “While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof” ([[Song.1.12|Song of Solomon 1:12]]).
Bible interpreters.
Carried away with delight.

notes.term: Abide in me, and I in you
His left hand is under my head
notes.note: [[Song.2.6|Song of Solomon 2:6]].

modern:
Here was sovereignty. Impatient spirits may fret and fume because they aren’t called to the highest places in the ministry; but, reader, let it be yours to rejoice that Jesus calls whom he wants. If he leaves me to be a doorkeeper in his house, I will cheerfully bless him for his grace in letting me do anything in his service. The call of Christ’s servants comes from above. Jesus stands on the mountain, forever above the world in holiness, earnestness, love and power. Those he calls must go up the mountain to him; they must try to rise to his level by living in constant communion with him. They may not be able to climb to academic honors or reach scholarly distinction, but like Moses they must go up into the mountain of God and have close fellowship with the unseen God, or they will never be fit to proclaim the gospel of peace. Jesus went off by himself to hold high fellowship with the Father, and we must enter the same divine companionship if we want to bless our fellow men. No wonder the apostles were clothed with power when they came down fresh from the mountain where Jesus was.

This morning we must try to climb the mountain of communion, so that there we may be ordained to the life’s work we are set apart for. Let’s not see anyone’s face today until we have seen Jesus. Time spent with him is invested at blessed interest. We too will cast out devils and work wonders if we go down into the world clothed with the divine energy that only Christ can give. It is no use going to the Lord’s battle until we are armed with heavenly weapons. We *must* see Jesus; this is essential. We will linger at the mercy-seat until he shows himself to us as he doesn’t to the world, and until we can truthfully say, “We were with him in the Holy Mount.”

notes.term: Calleth unto him whom he would
notes.note: Jesus went up a mountain and chose the twelve apostles, “that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach” ([[Mark.3.13-Mark.3.14|Mark 3:13–14]]).
God’s right and power to rule and to choose freely, answering to no one.
“I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” ([[Ps.84.10|Psalm 84:10]]).
University prizes for learning Latin and Greek. Spurgeon himself never went to college.
Distinction as a scholar.
In older English, conversation and fellowship.

notes.term: Like Moses go up into the mount of God

notes.note: Clothed and ready for action, like a robe tucked into a belt.
The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, where God met with his people; a picture of coming to God in prayer.

notes.term: Manifest himself unto us as he doth not unto the world
notes.note: “Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?” ([[John.14.22|John 14:22]]).

notes.term: We were with him in the Holy Mount
notes.note: Peter remembering the Transfiguration ([[2Pet.1.18|2 Peter 1:18]]).

modern: While I was preparing this book, this particular phrase came back to me so often that, to be rid of its constant nagging, I decided to give it a page. The evening wolf, maddened by a day of hunger, was fiercer and more ravenous than he would have been in the morning. Couldn’t this furious creature stand for our doubts and fears after a day of distraction, losses in business, and perhaps unkind taunts from other people? How our thoughts howl in our ears, “Where is now thy God?” How ravenous and greedy they are, swallowing up every comforting thought and staying as hungry as before. Great Shepherd, kill these evening wolves, and tell your sheep to lie down in green pastures, undisturbed by unbelief that is never satisfied. How like evening wolves the demons of hell are! When the flock of Christ is in a cloudy, dark day and their sun seems to be going down, they hurry in to tear and devour. They will hardly attack the Christian in the daylight of faith, but in the gloom of inner conflict they fall on him. You who laid down your life for the sheep, keep them safe from the wolf’s fangs.

False teachers who cunningly and busily hunt for the precious life, devouring people with their lies, are as dangerous and hateful as evening wolves. Darkness is their element, deceit is their character, destruction is their end. We are in most danger from them when they wear sheep’s clothing. Blessed is the one who is kept from them, for thousands fall prey to the savage wolves that get inside the fold of the church.

What a wonder of grace it is when fierce persecutors are converted! Then the wolf lives with the lamb, and people of cruel, uncontrollable temper become gentle and teachable. O Lord, convert many like that; we will pray for them tonight.

notes.note: The prophet describing the Babylonian army: “Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves” ([[Hab.1.8|Habakkuk 1:8]]).
Persistent nagging.
The enemies’ taunt in [[Ps.42.10|Psalm 42:10]].
“He maketh me to lie down in green pastures” ([[Ps.23.2|Psalm 23:2]]).
Never satisfied.
Devils, demons.

notes.term: Thou who hast laid down thy life for the sheep
notes.note: “The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” ([[John.10.11|John 10:11]]).
“The adulteress will hunt for the precious life” ([[Prov.6.26|Proverbs 6:26]]).
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” ([[Matt.7.15|Matthew 7:15]]).
Paul to the Ephesian elders: “grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock” ([[Acts.20.29|Acts 20:29]]). Grievous means savage.

notes.term: The wolf dwells with the lamb
notes.note: “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb” ([[Isa.11.6|Isaiah 11:6]]).

modern:
The Christian, while in the world, is not to be of the world. He should stand apart from it in *the great purpose of his life*. To him, “to live,” should be “Christ.” Whether he eats or drinks or whatever he does, he should do it all to God’s glory. You may store up treasure; but store it up in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves don’t break in and steal. You may work hard to be rich; but let your ambition be to be “rich in faith,” and in good works. You may have pleasure; but when you are merry, sing psalms and make music in your hearts to the Lord.

In your *spirit*, as well as in your aim, you should be different from the world. Waiting humbly before God, always aware of his presence, delighting in fellowship with him and seeking to know his will, you will prove that you are of heavenly descent. And you should be separate from the world in your *actions*. If a thing is right, it must be done, even if you lose by it; if it is wrong, you must scorn the sin for your Master’s sake, even if you would gain by it. You must have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. Live up to your high calling and dignity.

Remember, Christian, that you are a son of the King of kings. So keep yourself unspotted by the world. Don’t soil the fingers that will soon sweep the strings of heaven’s harps; don’t let these eyes, which will soon see the King in his beauty, become windows of lust; don’t let those feet, which will soon walk the golden streets, be dirtied in muddy places; don’t let those hearts, which before long are to be filled with heaven and overflow with ecstatic joy, be filled with pride and bitterness.

notes.note: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord” ([[2Cor.6.17|2 Corinthians 6:17]]).

notes.term: In the world, is not to be of the world
notes.note: Jesus said of his disciples, “They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world” ([[John.17.16|John 17:16]]).
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” ([[Phil.1.21|Philippians 1:21]]).
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” ([[1Cor.10.31|1 Corinthians 10:31]]).
[[Matt.6.20|Matthew 6:20]].

notes.term: Sing psalms and make melody in your hearts
notes.note: “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” ([[Jas.5.13|James 5:13]]); “making melody in your heart to the Lord” ([[Eph.5.19|Ephesians 5:19]]).
“And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” ([[Eph.5.11|Ephesians 5:11]]). To reprove is to expose and rebuke.
The harps of heaven ([[Rev.14.2|Revelation 14:2]]).
“Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty” ([[Isa.33.17|Isaiah 33:17]]).
Muddy.

modern:
The world’s hostility toward the people of Christ is very bitter. People will forgive a thousand faults in others, but they will blow up the most trivial offense in the followers of Jesus. Instead of uselessly regretting this, let’s turn it to good use. Since so many are watching for us to stumble, let this be a special reason for walking very carefully before God. If we live carelessly, the sharp-eyed world will soon see it, and with its hundred tongues it will spread the story, exaggerated and dressed up by the eagerness of slander. They will shout in triumph, “Aha! So would we have it! See how these Christians act! They are hypocrites to a man.” So much damage will be done to the cause of Christ, and much insult offered to his name.

The cross of Christ is in itself an offense to the world; let’s be careful that we add no offense of our own. It is “to the Jews a stumblingblock”: let’s see to it that we put no stumbling blocks where there are enough already. “To the Greeks it is foolishness”: let’s not add our folly to sharpen the scorn with which the worldly-wise mock the gospel. How watchful we should be over ourselves! How strict with our consciences! In the presence of opponents who will twist our best deeds, and question our motives where they can’t find fault with our actions, how careful we should be!

Pilgrims travel through Vanity Fair as suspected persons. Not only are we under watch, but there are more spies than we know of. The spying goes on everywhere, at home and away. If we fall into the enemy’s hands we might sooner expect generosity from a wolf, or mercy from a demon, than any patience with our weaknesses from people who spice their unbelief toward God with scandals against his people. O Lord, lead us always, or our enemies will trip us up!

notes.term: Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness because of mine enemies
notes.note: “…make thy way straight before my face” ([[Ps.5.8|Psalm 5:8]]).
Hostility.
Limping; stumbling. “All my familiars watched for my halting” ([[Jer.20.10|Jeremiah 20:10]]).
Sharp-eyed, like the lynx, a wild cat famous for its keen sight.
Decorated; made showy.
“But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” ([[1Cor.1.23|1 Corinthians 1:23]]). A stumbling block is something that trips people up.
Call into question.
Find fault with.
Careful, watchful.
In Bunyan’s *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, the town fair where everything worldly is for sale. Christian and Faithful were mocked, arrested and put on trial there, and Faithful was put to death.
Unbelief.

modern:
*Your Lord is very jealous of your love*, believer. Did he choose you? He can’t bear for you to choose another. Did he buy you with his own blood? He can’t stand for you to think that you are your own, or that you belong to this world. He loved you with such a love that he wouldn’t stay in heaven without you; he would sooner die than let you perish, and he can’t bear for anything to stand between your heart’s love and himself.

*He is very jealous of your trust*. He won’t let you trust in an arm of flesh. He can’t bear for you to dig out broken cisterns when the overflowing fountain is always free to you. When we lean on him he is glad; but when we shift our dependence onto something else, when we rely on our own wisdom or the wisdom of a friend—worst of all, when we trust in any works of our own—he is displeased, and will discipline us to bring us back to himself.

*He is also very jealous of our company*. There should be no one we talk with as much as with Jesus. To abide in him alone: this is true love. But to commune with the world, to find enough comfort in our earthly pleasures, even to prefer the company of our fellow Christians to private fellowship with him—this grieves our jealous Lord. He would gladly have us abide in him and enjoy constant fellowship with himself; and many of the trials he sends us are meant to wean our hearts from created things and fix them more closely on himself.

Let this jealousy, which would keep us near to Christ, *also be a comfort* to us. If he loves us so much that he cares like this about *our* love, we can be sure he will let nothing harm us, and will protect us from all our enemies. Oh, that we may have grace today to keep our hearts in sacred faithfulness for our Beloved alone, with a holy jealousy shutting our eyes to all the charms of the world!

notes.note: “God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth” ([[Nah.1.2|Nahum 1:2]]). God’s jealousy is the fierce love of a husband who won’t share his bride’s heart with another.

modern: Faith triumphs in trial. When reason is thrown into the inner prison with her feet fastened in the stocks, faith makes the dungeon walls ring with her cheerful notes as she cries, “I will sing of mercy and of judgment. Unto thee, O Lord, will I sing.” Faith pulls the black mask off the face of trouble and finds the angel underneath. Faith looks up at the cloud and sees that

There is something to sing about even in God’s judgments toward us. For, first, the trial is *not as heavy as it might have been*; next, the trouble is *not as severe as we deserved to bear*; and our affliction is *not as crushing as the burden others have to carry*. Faith sees that in her worst sorrow there is nothing of punishment; there isn’t a drop of God’s anger in it; it is all sent in love. Faith sees love gleaming like a jewel on the chest of an angry God. Faith says of her grief, “This is a badge of honour, for the child must feel the rod”; and then she sings of the sweet result of her sorrows, because they work for her spiritual good. More than that, says Faith, “These light afflictions, which are but for a moment, work out for me a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.” So Faith rides out on the black horse, conquering and to conquer, trampling down earthly reasoning and the feelings of the flesh, and chanting songs of victory in the thick of the fight.

modern: This teaches us that the *comfort* one person finds may often prove useful to another, just as wells would be used by the travelers who came after. We read some book full of comfort, which is like Jonathan’s rod, dripping with honey. Ah! we think, our brother has been here before us, and dug this well for us as well as for himself. Many a “Night of Weeping,” “Midnight Harmonies,” an “Eternal Day,” “A Crook in the Lot,” a “Comfort for Mourners,” has been a well dug by a pilgrim for himself, but has proved just as useful to others. We notice this especially in the Psalms, such as the one that begins, “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” Travelers have been delighted to see a human footprint on a barren shore, and we love to see the markers left by pilgrims as we pass through the valley of tears.

The pilgrims dig the well, but, strangely enough, it fills from the top instead of the bottom. We use the means, but the blessing doesn’t spring from the means. We dig a well, but heaven fills it with rain. The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but safety is from the Lord. The means are connected with the result, but they don’t produce it by themselves. See here: the rain fills the pools, so that the wells become useful as reservoirs for the water. The work isn’t wasted, but it doesn’t replace God’s help either.

Grace may well be compared to rain: for its purity, for its refreshing and life-giving influence, for its coming only from above, and for the sovereign freedom with which it is given or held back. May our readers have showers of blessing, and may the wells they have dug be filled with water! Oh, what are means and ordinances without the smile of heaven! They are clouds without rain, and pools without water. O God of love, open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing on us!

modern: Notice *the condescension* in this fact. This Man, who towers above all other men, holy, harmless, undefiled and separate from sinners—*this* Man receives sinners. This Man, who is none other than the eternal God, before whom angels veil their faces—*this* Man receives sinners. It would take an angel’s tongue to describe such a mighty stoop of love. That any of *us* should be willing to seek the lost is nothing wonderful; they are our own kind. But that he, the offended God, against whom the wrong was committed, should take on himself the form of a servant and bear the sin of many, and then be willing to receive the vilest of the vile: this is marvelous.

“This Man receiveth sinners”; not so that they may stay sinners, though. He receives them in order to pardon their sins, justify them, cleanse their hearts by his purifying word, keep their souls by the Holy Spirit living in them, and enable them to serve him, to show his praise and to have fellowship with him. He receives sinners into his heart’s love; he takes them from the dunghill and wears them as jewels in his crown; he snatches them like burning sticks from the fire and keeps them as costly monuments of his mercy. No one is as precious in Jesus’ sight as the sinners he died for. When Jesus receives sinners, he doesn’t have some reception area outside, no casual ward where he kindly puts them up the way people do passing beggars. He opens the golden gates of his royal heart and receives the sinner right into himself. Yes, he brings the humble penitent into personal union with himself and makes him a member of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. There was never a reception like this! This fact is still sure this evening: he is still receiving sinners. If only sinners would receive him!

modern: Jesus was the Lord High Admiral of the sea that night, and his presence kept the whole fleet safe. It is good to sail with Jesus, even if it is in a little ship. When we sail in Christ’s company we can’t be sure of fair weather, for great storms may toss the very boat that carries the Lord himself, and we mustn’t expect the sea to be calmer around our little boat. If we go with Jesus we must be content to fare as he fares; when the waves are rough to him, they will be rough to us. It is through storm and tossing that we will come to land, as he did before us.

When the storm swept over Galilee’s dark lake, every face grew black and every heart dreaded shipwreck. When all human help was useless, the sleeping Savior got up and with a word turned the riot of the storm into the deep quiet of a calm; then the little boats were at rest as well as the one that carried the Lord. Jesus is the star of the sea; and though there is sorrow on the sea, when Jesus is on it there is joy too. May our hearts make Jesus their anchor, their rudder, their lighthouse, their lifeboat and their harbor. His church is the Admiral’s flagship; let’s keep pace with her and cheer her officers with our company. He himself is the great attraction; let’s follow always in his wake, watch his signals, steer by his chart, and never be afraid while he is within call.

Not one ship in the fleet will be wrecked; the great Commodore will steer every vessel safely to the desired harbor. By faith we will slip our mooring for another day’s voyage, and sail out with Jesus onto a sea of trouble. Winds and waves won’t spare us, but they all obey him; so whatever squalls come outside, faith will feel a blessed calm inside. He is always at the center of the weather-beaten company; let’s rejoice in him. His ship has reached the harbor, and so will ours.

modern:
David’s grief over sin was bitter. Its effects showed in his body: “his bones waxed old”; “his moisture was turned into the drought of summer.” He could find no remedy until he made a full confession before the throne of heavenly grace. He tells us that for a time he kept silent, and his heart filled more and more with grief. Like a mountain lake whose outlet is blocked, his soul swelled with torrents of sorrow. He invented excuses; he tried to turn his thoughts elsewhere, but it was all useless. His anguish gathered like a festering sore, and since he wouldn’t use the lancet of confession, his spirit was full of torment and knew no rest.

At last it came to this: he must return to his God in humble repentance, or die outright. So he hurried to the mercy-seat, and there unrolled the scroll of his sins before the all-seeing One, admitting all the evil of his ways in words like those you read in the fifty-first and the other penitential psalms. Having done this, a thing so simple and yet so hard for pride, he at once received the token of God’s forgiveness. The bones that had been broken were made to rejoice, and he came out of his private room to sing of the blessedness of the man whose transgression is forgiven.

See the value of a confession of sin worked by grace! It is to be prized above all price, for wherever there is a genuine, grace-given confession, mercy is freely given—not because the repentance and confession *deserve* mercy, but for *Christ’s sake*. Blessed be God, there is always healing for the broken heart; the fountain is always flowing to cleanse us from our sins. Truly, O Lord, you are a God “ready to pardon!” So we will acknowledge our sins.
